job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied mechanical engineering at a technical university in Stuttgart, and since September I've been a design engineer at a family-owned firm in Heilbronn that makes gearboxes for tractors. I draw parts on CAD, I check them against drawings from the older engineers, and on Thursdays I go to the workshop floor and watch the machinists make what I drew. I rent a room in a flat with my friend Marta from church, and I go to my parents' farm every second weekend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love Thursdays on the floor, when a machinist tells me my part won't fit and he's right. What wears me out is that I'm the only woman in the design office, and I get tired of explaining myself. I owe about 20,000 for the degree, and I have roughly seven weeks of spending in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. I've never used any of these AI programs, and I don't plan to start. A gearbox either runs or it doesn't, and no chatbot has stood in a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel steady. Our firm has been in the same family for sixty years, and my boss says it'll be there for sixty more. My pay is fair, and my parents would take me back to the farm in a pinch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, finish my first year, and ask to be taught by Herr Brandt, the oldest engineer, before he retires. I'd put 150 a month on the loan, which I'd like gone before I think about a wedding. I'd carry on going home on alternate weekends to help with the harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit lonely in the office, but that's not about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone plan and my train pass, I'd get a lift from Marta. I wouldn't cut what I give at church, though, because that's not a question for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Marta someone you'd go to for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and my mother. When I was in my last year at university she sent me fifty euros in an envelope with a prayer card. I'd never take more than I need, but it was good to know.

say: I'd say that's what I expected; a gearbox either runs or it doesn't, and **no chatbot** has stood in a workshop.
I don't use AI programs and **don't plan to**.
think: Privately I feel **steady**, because our firm has been in the same family for sixty years.
My parents would take me back to the **farm** in a pinch.
do: Finish my first year and learn from the oldest engineer, **Herr Brandt**, before he retires.
Put **150 a month** on the loan and keep going home every second weekend.
feel: **Content**, though a bit lonely in the office.
S0.quote: A gearbox either runs or it doesn't, and no chatbot has stood in a workshop.
fieldNote: Her calm comes from a **family-owned firm** and her parents' farm as a fallback.
Her resistance is practical and moral: she trusts the workshop floor, not the screen.
The loneliness she mentions is about being the only woman, not technology.

steps.text: Learn gearbox design from Herr Brandt before he retires
Pay 150 a month on the student loan
Go home to my parents' farm every second weekend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through this before. When CAD came in, the old engineers said drawing was finished, and we still have a design office. I'd say the answer is training people properly, not new government programmes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy. The design office work, the checking and drawing, is exactly what they say will go, and I'm the youngest there. My boss might decide a smaller office is fine and keep only the older engineers. I'm at the bottom of the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the workshop floor more, because that's where design is learned and where software can't follow. I'd ask my boss about the firm's apprenticeship scheme so I understand every machine. I wouldn't use the AI program myself unless he told me to, and then I'd do it by hand first and compare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not fear exactly, but a stone in my shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do it by hand first. Isn't that slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is slow, and I know my colleagues might get ahead of me. But if a drawing goes wrong, it's my name on the drawing, and a gearbox that fails on a farm is somebody's whole season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father say about the idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says a farmer who stops looking at the soil will lose the field. I think that's the same thing, whatever kind of machine you've got.

say: I'd say we've been through this before; when CAD came in, people said **drawing was finished**.
The answer is **training**, not new government programmes.
think: The checking and drawing in the design office is what they say will go, and I'm the **youngest** there.
My boss might keep a smaller office of **older engineers**.
do: Spend more time on the **workshop floor** and ask about the apprenticeship scheme.
Use AI only if the boss orders it, and do the **work by hand** first.
feel: **Uneasy**; not fear exactly, but a stone in my shoe.
S1.quote: If a drawing goes wrong, it's my name on the drawing, and a gearbox that fails on a farm is somebody's whole season.
fieldNote: She values **accountability**, her name on the drawing, over speed, which makes her resistant to the tools.
Her **father's farm saying** about looking at the soil guides how she thinks about checking.
She doesn't ask for government help; she wants training and a place on the floor.

steps.text: Spend two days a week on the workshop floor learning every machine
Draw every part by hand first and then compare
Wait for my boss to decide before trying any AI program

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast, and I'd not want a government to answer it with handouts. I'd want firms and families to do their part, and I'd say so at church and to my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be alarmed. If AI can do almost any thinking work, my design job is gone in 2028, and my degree is worth little. The robots would arrive in 2031 for the workshop floor too, and then everything I love is gone. I'd be 24 with a loan and no job, and my parents' farm can't support me forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I can, sell what I don't need, and move home to the farm for a year. I'd work the land and look for any job that needs hands, like a repair or a trade. I'd also talk to our pastor about what the church can do, and ask my parents whether the loan is something we handle together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep. I'd probably pray more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would say you're always welcome here, and she'd put the kettle on. My mother would say work is more than a wage, and then she'd go out and check the cows, because that's what she does when she's worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but only to bridge a gap. I'd want to give back as soon as I could.

say: I'd say two years is too fast, but I **don't want handouts** as the answer.
I'd tell friends that **firms and families** must do their part.
think: If AI does almost any thinking work, my design job is gone in 2028 and my **degree is worth little**.
My parents' farm can't support me **forever**.
do: Move home to the **farm** for a year and work the land.
Talk to our **pastor** and ask my parents to handle the loan together.
feel: **Alarmed**; I wouldn't sleep, and I'd probably pray more.
S2.quote: My mother would say work is more than a wage, and then she'd go out and check the cows, because that's what she does when she's worried.
fieldNote: Her private fear is stark, but her public line is about **families and firms**, not state help.
The farm is both a refuge and a **pride issue**; she wants to give back quickly.
Her mother's way of coping is a model for how she'd behave.

steps.text: Move home to my parents' farm for a year
Ask the pastor and my parents for help with the loan
Sell what I don't need and cut every non-essential cost
Look for a repair or trade job that needs hands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that families can plan, so we should start talking about it now. I'd also say firms like ours should train young people in practical trades alongside engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm anxious but not desperate. By 2031 I'd be 27, and I'd like to be married with a home by then. The workshop side keeps its value for three more years, so I think my place is on the floor, not at the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from design towards production engineering, because I'd rather run machines than draw them. I'd save 300 a month for a house deposit and go on living modestly. And I'd start going to the apprenticeship board at the firm, so I know what trades are most in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but hopeful. Five years is enough to build a life on, if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a wedding and a home in the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd like to have a family, and I'd want the home paid for before anything changes. My plan is to marry a man from my church, a good worker, and build a house on my parents' land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI timeline change when you'd want children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe slightly. I'd want a bit more savings first, but I wouldn't delay because of a computer. Children are the point of the work, not the other way round.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for **families to plan**.
I'd say firms like ours should train young people in **practical trades**.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27 and would like to be **married with a home**.
The workshop side keeps its value for three more years, so my place is on the **floor**.
do: Move from design towards **production engineering** and run machines.
Save **300 a month** for a house deposit and look at the apprenticeship board.
feel: A bit **anxious** but hopeful; five years is enough to build a life on.
S3.quote: Children are the point of the work, not the other way round.
fieldNote: Her plan links **work, marriage and land**, and she won't let the timeline decide when to have children.
She picks production engineering because the floor holds value for **three more years**.
She is anxious but hopeful, which fits her traditional values.

steps.text: Ask to move from design to production engineering
Save 300 a month for a house deposit
Plan a wedding and a house on my parents' land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good chunk of time, and families and communities can adjust if they get on with it. I'd tell people not to wait for a politician to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly steady. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married, maybe with two children, and a senior engineer in a trade I understand. The change would arrive in a life that already has roots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the firm, work towards a senior role, and save for a house on my parents' land. I'd teach apprentices on the floor, because teaching is how you pass on a trade. I'd still not use AI myself if I didn't have to, and I might learn it slowly if my boss asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit proud. It's the version where a person can plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think refusing AI would still work in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, honestly. If everyone else used it, I'd have to learn at some point, because I'd be silly not to. But I'd choose when, and I'd keep my own judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger apprentice about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machine first, then the tool. I'd tell them the same way my old teacher told me, over a cup of coffee on the floor.

say: I'd say ten years is a good chunk of time and **communities can adjust** if they get on with it.
I'd tell people **not to wait** for a politician.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married, and a **senior engineer** in a trade I understand.
Refusing AI may not work forever, so I'd learn it at a **time I choose**.
do: Work towards a **senior role** and save for a house on my parents' land.
Teach **apprentices** on the floor and learn AI slowly if my boss asks.
feel: **Steady**, a bit proud; it's the version where a person can plan a life.
S4.quote: Learn the machine first, then the tool.
fieldNote: Her mood stays **uneasy**, not calm, because loan and being the only woman still weigh on her.
She admits resistance might not last, and wants to **choose when** to learn.
Teaching apprentices is how she sees her future.

steps.text: Work towards a senior design role at the firm
Save for a house on my parents' land
Teach apprentices on the workshop floor
Learn an AI tool only when my boss asks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there would be no time to build a home and no time for the church or my family to catch up. What would help is a firm that keeps people on and trains them, a family to lean on, and a chance to learn a trade that needs hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against new things. I'm against being told to give up what I know before I've had the chance to see it work.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I'm against being told to give up what I know before I've had the chance to see it work.
portrait: Olga is a 22-year-old **mechanical engineer** in her first job at a family-owned gearbox firm in Heilbronn, owing about 20,000.
She is resistant, **never uses AI tools**, and trusts the workshop floor, her father's farm sayings and her church.
Her traditional, free-market outlook favours work, family and apprenticeships over **handouts**, and she wants to build a home on her parents' land.
She is steady at the plateau, alarmed at two years and anxious at five, with ten bringing back an **uneasy** steadiness.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because there'd be no time to build a home or for her family to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A firm that keeps people on, a **family to lean on**, and a chance to learn a trade.
